pr: Dear heavenly Father, help us hold on to our faith in You in the midst of suffering, and not turn away from You because of circumstances or what people say. When we face trials, add strength to us, so that we believe You still reign. Give us compassionate hearts too, so that we learn to stay beside those who are suffering and bring them comfort and hope through love. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

t: God Allows Us to Pour Out Our Pain to Him
v: After this Job opened his mouth, and cursed the day of his birth.
Job answered:
“Let the day perish in which I was born, the night which said, ‘There is a boy conceived.’
Let that day be darkness. Don’t let God from above seek for it, neither let the light shine on it.
Let darkness and the shadow of death claim it for their own. Let a cloud dwell on it. Let all that makes the day black terrify it.
As for that night, let thick darkness seize on it. Let it not rejoice among the days of the year. Let it not come into the number of the months.
Behold, let that night be barren. Let no joyful voice come therein.
Let them curse it who curse the day, who are ready to rouse up leviathan.
Let the stars of its twilight be dark. Let it look for light, but have none, neither let it see the eyelids of the morning,
because it didn’t shut up the doors of my mother’s womb, nor did it hide trouble from my eyes.
“Why didn’t I die from the womb? Why didn’t I give up the spirit when my mother bore me?
Why did the knees receive me? Or why the breast, that I should nurse?
For now I should have lain down and been quiet. I should have slept, then I would have been at rest,
with kings and counselors of the earth, who built up waste places for themselves;
or with princes who had gold, who filled their houses with silver;
or as a hidden untimely birth I had not been, as infants who never saw light.
There the wicked cease from troubling. There the weary are at rest.
There the prisoners are at ease together. They don’t hear the voice of the taskmaster.
The small and the great are there. The servant is free from his master.
“Why is light given to him who is in misery, life to the bitter in soul,
who long for death, but it doesn’t come; and dig for it more than for hidden treasures,
who rejoice exceedingly, and are glad, when they can find the grave?
Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?
For my sighing comes before I eat. My groanings are poured out like water.
For the thing which I fear comes on me, that which I am afraid of comes to me.
I am not at ease, neither am I quiet, neither do I have rest; but trouble comes.”
b: This chapter begins the dialogue between Job and his friends. After seven days of silence, Job finally spoke. He did not curse God, but he cursed the day he was born, expressing the deep pain in his heart. He asked again and again, “Why was I born?” “Why am I still alive?”—showing that his suffering had drained him of the strength to go on living. Yet even in great despair, Job still did not forsake God; instead, he poured out the most honest pain of his heart to God.

Job’s lament shows us that the Bible does not deny human grief and tears. God allows His children to cry out in lament in their pain, and He is willing to listen to their deepest cries. True faith is not the absence of tears, but coming before God even while weeping, and pouring out the bitterness of our hearts to Him.

This chapter reminds us that in life we sometimes meet suffering we cannot understand, and may even lose hope. But even so, God had not left Job, nor had He stopped ruling over his life. When we reach the lowest valley of life, we can still honestly pour out our hearts to God, trusting that in the end He will bring His comfort, healing, and hope.
ah: What God Teaches Us in This Chapter
a: God Allows Us to Pour Out Our Pain to Him
Honest prayer can bring our deepest sorrow before God.
We Can Keep Trusting God in Suffering
Even when we do not understand why, do not stop seeking God.
God Knows Our Weakness and Sees Our Tears
God has not abandoned those who suffer; He is still with us.
q: How can I bring the pain and sorrow in my heart openly before God?
How can I still choose to trust God when I do not understand what He is doing?
How can I come alongside people who are in pain so that they feel God’s love and hope?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, when we fall into pain, disappointment, and darkness, help us, like Job, to bring the bitterness of our hearts honestly before You rather than drifting away from You. Comfort those who grieve, uphold those who are weak, and grant the hope and peace that come from You, so that we believe the night will pass and Your grace will never leave us. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

t: Do Not Be Quick to Equate Suffering with Sin
v: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered,
“If someone ventures to talk with you, will you be grieved? But who can withhold himself from speaking?
Behold, you have instructed many, you have strengthened the weak hands.
Your words have supported him who was falling, you have made the feeble knees firm.
But now it has come to you, and you faint. It touches you, and you are troubled.
Isn’t your piety your confidence? Isn’t the integrity of your ways your hope?
“Remember, now, who ever perished, being innocent? Or where were the upright cut off?
According to what I have seen, those who plow iniquity and sow trouble, reap the same.
By the breath of God they perish. By the blast of his anger are they consumed.
The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the fierce lion, the teeth of the young lions, are broken.
The old lion perishes for lack of prey. The cubs of the lioness are scattered abroad.
“Now a thing was secretly brought to me. My ear received a whisper of it.
In thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men,
fear came on me, and trembling, which made all my bones shake.
Then a spirit passed before my face. The hair of my flesh stood up.
It stood still, but I couldn’t discern its appearance. A form was before my eyes. Silence, then I heard a voice, saying,
‘Shall mortal man be more just than God? Shall a man be more pure than his Maker?
Behold, he puts no trust in his servants. He charges his angels with error.
How much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed before the moth!
Between morning and evening they are destroyed. They perish forever without any regarding it.
Isn’t their tent cord plucked up within them? They die, and that without wisdom.’
b: This chapter begins the first round of dialogue between Job and his friends. Eliphaz first acknowledges that Job had comforted many people in the past, but now has grown discouraged because of his suffering. Then he presents his central argument: he believes suffering must be the result of sin, that the innocent do not meet such disasters, and so he implies that Job must be hiding some sin. Eliphaz even cites a vision he had received, stressing that no human is perfect before God, in order to support his argument.

However, Eliphaz’s greatest error was not in exalting God’s justice, but in misapplying the truth. He treated a “general pattern” as an “absolute rule,” assuming all suffering is God’s judgment on sin, and so he misunderstood Job’s situation. We readers know that Job was suffering not because of sin, but because of a test of faith that God had allowed; so Eliphaz’s conclusion did not match the facts.

This chapter reminds us that truth lacking love and the full picture can wound those who suffer. When we face other people’s suffering, we should not rush to condemn or speculate about the cause. Instead, we should keep a humble heart, acknowledge that God’s works are higher than human understanding, and learn to stay beside others with compassion and wisdom.
ah: What God Teaches Us in This Chapter
a: Do Not Be Quick to Equate Suffering with Sin
What happens to a person does not necessarily mean God is judging them.
Truth Must Go Together with Love and Humility
Before quoting the truth, first learn to feel what the sufferer is going through.
God’s Works Are Higher Than Human Judgment
Do not judge God’s work with a limited perspective.
q: How can I avoid judging people who are suffering by my own ideas?
How can I accompany people facing hardship with love and wisdom?
How can I learn to trust that God’s works are beyond my understanding and judgment?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, give us wisdom and humility, so that we do not judge what others go through by our own understanding. Help us, when we comfort those who suffer, to stay beside them more with love, compassion, and prayer, rather than rushing to conclusions. And help us believe that Your ways are higher than our ways, and Your thoughts higher than our thoughts. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

t: Though Life Has Troubles, Entrust Everything to God
v: “Call now; is there any who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?
For resentment kills the foolish man, and jealousy kills the simple.
I have seen the foolish taking root, but suddenly I cursed his habitation.
His children are far from safety. They are crushed in the gate. Neither is there any to deliver them,
whose harvest the hungry eat up, and take it even out of the thorns. The snare gapes for their substance.
For affliction doesn’t come out of the dust, neither does trouble spring out of the ground;
but man is born to trouble, as the sparks fly upward.
“But as for me, I would seek God. I would commit my cause to God,
who does great things that can’t be fathomed, marvelous things without number;
who gives rain on the earth, and sends waters on the fields;
so that he sets up on high those who are low, those who mourn are exalted to safety.
He frustrates the plans of the crafty, so that their hands can’t perform their enterprise.
He takes the wise in their own craftiness; the counsel of the cunning is carried headlong.
They meet with darkness in the day time, and grope at noonday as in the night.
But he saves from the sword of their mouth, even the needy from the hand of the mighty.
So the poor has hope, and injustice shuts her mouth.
“Behold, happy is the man whom God corrects. Therefore do not despise the chastening of the Almighty.
For he wounds and binds up. He injures and his hands make whole.
He will deliver you in six troubles; yes, in seven no evil will touch you.
In famine he will redeem you from death; in war, from the power of the sword.
You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, neither will you be afraid of destruction when it comes.
You will laugh at destruction and famine, neither will you be afraid of the animals of the earth.
For you will be allied with the stones of the field. The animals of the field will be at peace with you.
You will know that your tent is in peace. You will visit your fold, and will miss nothing.
You will know also that your offspring will be great, your offspring as the grass of the earth.
You will come to your grave in a full age, like a shock of grain comes in its season.
Behold, we have researched it. It is so. Hear it, and know it for your good.”
b: This chapter concludes Eliphaz’s first speech. He urges Job to turn to God and points out that human life is naturally full of trouble. However, he still believes Job’s suffering is God’s discipline, so he encourages Job to accept God’s chastening, trusting that God will in the end heal, bless, and restore everything. Much of what Eliphaz says about God’s attributes—such as God showing grace, healing, saving, and watching over the righteous—is true in itself, but he wrongly applies it to Job’s circumstances.

Eliphaz’s biggest problem is that he was certain Job must have sinned and was therefore being punished by God. He did not know that Job’s suffering was not because of sin, but was a test God had allowed. So although he quoted many correct theological ideas, his lack of a full understanding of God’s will made him a mistaken comforter to Job.

This chapter reminds us that knowing the truth is important, but even more important is applying the truth according to God’s heart. We cannot judge a person’s spiritual condition by outward circumstances, nor can we explain all suffering as God’s discipline. Those who truly belong to God must learn to keep a humble heart and trust that God’s wisdom far surpasses human judgment.
ah: What God Teaches Us in This Chapter
a: Though Life Has Troubles, Entrust Everything to God
God is our greatest support in times of trouble.
Do Not Casually Judge the Cause of Suffering
Not all suffering is caused by sin or by God’s chastening.
Truth Must Be Applied Rightly According to God’s Heart
Even correct truth, if misused, can hurt people.
q: How can I learn to entrust everything to God in times of difficulty?
How can I avoid judging others’ spiritual condition by appearances or circumstances?
How can I use truth and love to comfort and help people who are suffering?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, thank You that You are our refuge in times of trouble. Help us to keep trusting You in difficulty and to entrust every burden to You. Give us heavenly wisdom too, so that we do not judge people by appearances, but serve others with love, truth, and humility, living lives that please You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

t: Holding Fast to God’s Word in Suffering
v: Then Job answered,
“Oh that my anguish were weighed, and all my calamity laid in the balances!
For now it would be heavier than the sand of the seas, therefore my words have been rash.
For the arrows of the Almighty are within me. My spirit drinks up their poison. The terrors of God set themselves in array against me.
Does the wild donkey bray when he has grass? Or does the ox low over his fodder?
Can that which has no flavor be eaten without salt? Or is there any taste in the white of an egg?
My soul refuses to touch them. They are as loathsome food to me.
“Oh that I might have my request, that God would grant the thing that I long for,
even that it would please God to crush me; that he would let loose his hand, and cut me off!
Let it still be my consolation, yes, let me exult in pain that doesn’t spare, that I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
What is my strength, that I should wait? What is my end, that I should be patient?
Is my strength the strength of stones? Or is my flesh of bronze?
Isn’t it that I have no help in me, that wisdom is driven away from me?
“To him who is ready to faint, kindness should be shown from his friend; even to him who forsakes the fear of the Almighty.
My brothers have dealt deceitfully as a brook, as the channel of brooks that pass away;
which are black by reason of the ice, in which the snow hides itself.
In the dry season, they vanish. When it is hot, they are consumed out of their place.
The caravans that travel beside them turn away. They go up into the waste, and perish.
The caravans of Tema looked. The companies of Sheba waited for them.
They were distressed because they were confident. They came there, and were confounded.
For now you are nothing. You see a terror, and are afraid.
Did I ever say, ‘Give to me’? or, ‘Offer a present for me from your substance’?
or, ‘Deliver me from the adversary’s hand’? or, ‘Redeem me from the hand of the oppressors’?
“Teach me, and I will hold my peace. Cause me to understand my error.
How forcible are words of uprightness! But your reproof, what does it reprove?
Do you intend to reprove words, since the speeches of one who is desperate are as wind?
Yes, you would even cast lots for the fatherless, and make merchandise of your friend.
Now therefore be pleased to look at me, for surely I will not lie to your face.
Please return. Let there be no injustice. Yes, return again. My cause is righteous.
Is there injustice on my tongue? Can’t my taste discern mischievous things?
b: This chapter is Job’s reply to Eliphaz. Job admits that his words have been rash, because his suffering is heavier than the sand of the sea; the arrows of the Almighty are within him, and the terrors of God are set in array against him. He says that a wild donkey does not bray when it has grass, nor an ox low over its fodder—his lament is not complaining without cause, but the cry of someone crushed under a weight he truly cannot bear. Job even asks God to crush him, yet he still holds on to one comfort: he has not denied the words of the Holy One.

Job then turns to his friends and speaks of his disappointment. He says that a man who is about to lose heart should receive kindness from his friend. Yet his friends have been like a brook, like streams that run dry; thirsty caravans come to the riverbank full of hope, only to find the bed long since dried up, and they are left confused and ashamed. Job has not asked his friends for gifts or to rescue him from his enemies; he only longs to be truly understood, and he begs them to show him where he has gone wrong.

This chapter reminds us that what suffering people need most is often not a set of correct doctrines, but a heart willing to sympathize. In extreme pain, a person’s words will often be rash; let us not seize on their words to argue, but hear the tears behind them. May we not be dry riverbeds, but let the love of Christ flow out of our hearts as living water for the weary.
ah: What God Teaches in This Chapter
a: Hold fast to God’s word even in suffering
Even in the deepest pain, not denying God’s word is the comfort of our hearts.
A friend’s greatest treasure is kindness and faithfulness
When someone is discouraged and weak, treating them with kindness matters more than giving answers.
Hear the pain behind the words
Sympathize with the weakness of those who suffer; do not just seize on their words to argue.
q: When I am in pain, how can I still hold fast to God’s word as my comfort?
How can I be “living water” that friends can rely on in their weakness, rather than a dried-up riverbed?
When others say rash things in their pain, how can I first show sympathy instead of rushing to argue?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You know our burdens and sympathize with our weaknesses. When we speak rashly in our pain, have mercy on us and help us still hold fast to Your word. Make us a stream that never runs dry in others’ lives, walking with the discouraged in the kindness and faithfulness of Christ, so that through us they may experience Your comfort. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

t: Life Is Short, So Look to the Eternal God
v: “Isn’t a man forced to labor on earth? Aren’t his days like the days of a hired hand?
As a servant who earnestly desires the shadow, as a hireling who looks for his wages,
so I am made to possess months of misery, wearisome nights are appointed to me.
When I lie down, I say, ‘When will I arise, and the night be gone?’ I toss and turn until the dawning of the day.
My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust. My skin closes up, and breaks out afresh.
My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle, and are spent without hope.
Oh remember that my life is a breath. My eye will no more see good.
The eye of him who sees me will see me no more. Your eyes will be on me, but I will not be.
As the cloud is consumed and vanishes away, so he who goes down to Sheol will come up no more.
He will return no more to his house, neither will his place know him any more.
“Therefore I will not keep silent. I will speak in the anguish of my spirit. I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.
Am I a sea, or a sea monster, that you put a guard over me?
When I say, ‘My bed will comfort me. My couch will ease my complaint,’
then you scare me with dreams and terrify me through visions,
so that my soul chooses strangling, death rather than my bones.
I loathe my life. I don’t want to live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are but a breath.
What is man, that you should magnify him, that you should set your mind on him,
that you should visit him every morning, and test him every moment?
How long will you not look away from me, nor leave me alone until I swallow down my spittle?
If I have sinned, what do I do to you, you watcher of men? Why have you set me as a mark for you, so that I am a burden to myself?
Why do you not pardon my disobedience, and take away my iniquity? For now will I lie down in the dust. You will seek me diligently, but I will not be.”
b: This chapter is Job’s lament. He describes human life as warfare on a battlefield and the toil of a hired laborer: by day there is no hope, and by night he tosses and turns until dawn. His body is clothed with worms; his skin closes up and then breaks out again. His days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle and are spent without hope. Job deeply feels the brevity and fragility of life, saying, “My life is a breath.”

In his pain, Job no longer speaks only to his friends, but turns to pour out his heart to God. He says, “I will not keep my mouth closed,” and speaks out all the anguish of his spirit and the bitterness of his soul. He even asks God, “What is man, that you should magnify him, that you should set your mind on him?” This line was originally a psalm’s praise of God’s grace, but Job, in his suffering, turns it into the pressure of being constantly examined by God with nowhere to hide. He asks God to pardon his transgression, because he feels he is about to lie down in the dust.

This chapter shows us that a person who fears God can also experience weakness, doubt, and struggle in suffering. Yet what is most precious about Job is that he never left God, but brought his most honest heart before Him. What is man? In God’s view, people are those He values and sets His mind on. Later, through Jesus Christ, God Himself came into the world, bearing our transgressions and taking away our iniquity, so that in our short lives we may have eternal hope.
ah: What God Teaches Us in This Chapter
a: Life Is Short, So Look to the Eternal God
Life is but a breath; only God is our everlasting support.
We Can Pour Out Our Hearts to God
God is willing to listen to our most honest and deepest cries.
God Sets His Mind on Us
God’s watchful gaze is not meant to crush us; it flows from His care and love.
q: When life feels short and full of toil, how can I view my life from an eternal perspective?
Am I willing to openly pour out the deepest anguish of my heart to God?
How does the line “What is man, that you should magnify him” help me see afresh how much God values me?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, our life is but a breath, and our days pass swiftly. Teach us to number our days, and to look to You, the Eternal One, in this short life. When we toss and turn sleepless in the night, help us not to shut our mouths and drift from You, but to pour out our hearts to You. Thank You for setting Your mind on us, forgiving our transgressions through the Lord Jesus, and giving us the hope of eternal life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

t: God Is Just, but His Ways Are Higher Than Human Formulas
v: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered,
“How long will you speak these things? Shall the words of your mouth be a mighty wind?
Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert righteousness?
If your children have sinned against him, he has delivered them into the hand of their disobedience.
If you want to seek God diligently, make your supplication to the Almighty.
If you were pure and upright, surely now he would awaken for you, and make the habitation of your righteousness prosperous.
Though your beginning was small, yet your latter end would greatly increase.
“Please inquire of past generations. Find out about the learning of their fathers.
(For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days on earth are a shadow.)
Shall they not teach you, tell you, and utter words out of their heart?
“Can the papyrus grow up without mire? Can the rushes grow without water?
While it is yet in its greenness, not cut down, it withers before any other reed.
So are the paths of all who forget God. The hope of the godless man will perish,
whose confidence will break apart, whose trust is a spider’s web.
He will lean on his house, but it will not stand. He will cling to it, but it will not endure.
He is green before the sun. His shoots go out along his garden.
His roots are wrapped around the rock pile. He sees the place of stones.
If he is destroyed from his place, then it will deny him, saying, ‘I have not seen you.’
Behold, this is the joy of his way. Out of the earth, others will spring.
“Behold, God will not cast away a blameless man, neither will he uphold the evildoers.
He will still fill your mouth with laughter, your lips with shouting.
Those who hate you will be clothed with shame. The tent of the wicked will be no more.”
b: This chapter is the first speech of Bildad the Shuhite. As soon as he opens his mouth, he accuses Job’s words of being like a mighty wind, and then he insists: “Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert righteousness?” He even says that Job’s children were punished because they had sinned against God. Bildad believes that if only Job would diligently seek God and be pure and upright, God would surely restore his prosperity.

Bildad uses papyrus, reeds, and a spider’s web as pictures of those who forget God: papyrus cannot grow without mire, and what the wicked trust in is as flimsy as a spider’s web. He cites the tradition of earlier generations, claiming that God will not cast away a blameless man, nor will He uphold evildoers. What he says about God’s justice is certainly true, but he turns this truth into a mechanical formula: suffering means sin, and prosperity means blessing.

This chapter reminds us that God is indeed just, but we cannot box in God’s works with our own limited experience. Bildad’s cruelest words were spoken to a father who had just lost ten children—telling him his children got what they deserved. When our hearts are filled with self-righteous “correctness,” we very easily lose compassion. Those who truly belong to God must see people from God’s perspective, keep a humble heart, and speak words that build up and comfort.
ah: What God Teaches Us in This Chapter
a: God Is Just, but His Ways Are Higher Than Human Formulas
Do not box in God’s sovereignty and wisdom with human experience.
Speak with Compassion and Gentleness
Truth separated from love can become a knife that wounds.
Only God Is a Secure Place to Lean
Anything we lean on apart from God is as fragile as a spider’s web.
q: Have I ever used a “cause-and-effect formula” to judge what someone else is going through?
How can I let my words carry compassion even while speaking the truth?
What fragile, spider-web supports in my life do I need to hand over to God?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, You are the righteous God, and Your judgments never go astray. Deliver us from self-righteous hearts, so that we do not judge others’ suffering by our own formulas. Let our words be full of grace and able to comfort wounded hearts. And help us not to lean on things as fragile as a spider’s web, but to rely on You alone. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
